section_1.title: Introduction: The Concept of Dimension
section_1.content: Define n-dimensional space (Rn). Briefly review the 2D circle and 3D sphere as precursors to n-spheres. Establish the distance formula (Euclidean norm) as the foundational constraint for points on a surface.
section_1.example: Visualize a 'Flatland' character moving from a 2D circle to a 3D bubble, then imagining a higher-dimensional 'hyper-bubble' defined by x₁² + x₂² + ... + xₙ² = r².

section_2.title: The Geometry of High-Dimensional Volume
section_2.content: Discuss the counter-intuitive behavior of volume as dimensions increase. Introduce the formula for the volume of an n-ball. Explain why, as n approaches infinity, the volume concentrated near the shell changes drastically.
section_2.example: Use an animation showing an orange: in 3D, most of the mass is inside. In 100D, almost all the volume of the hyper-orange is concentrated in the thin 'peel' near the surface.

section_3.title: The 'Curse' and 'Blessing' of Dimensionality
section_3.content: Contrast the behavior of the n-ball with the n-cube (hypercube). Explain that a sphere inscribed in a cube becomes increasingly 'lost' in the corners of the cube as dimensions rise.
section_3.example: A squirrel attempting to hide an acorn in the center of a hyper-room: in high dimensions, the corners of the room grow so far away that the 'center' becomes a void.

section_4.title: Application: Data Science and Machine Learning
section_4.content: Connect high-dimensional spheres to modern technology. Explain how high-dimensional geometry is used to define similarity (Cosine similarity) and clustering in AI models.
section_4.example: A recommendation algorithm treats a user's preferences as a point in 1,000-dimensional space; 'neighbors' on a hyper-sphere represent users with similar tastes.

section_5.title: Conclusion: Summary and Visualization
section_5.content: Recap the main takeaway: intuition from 3D space fails in high dimensions. Encourage students to rely on algebraic constraints rather than physical visualization.
section_5.example: Final slide: A 3D projection of a 4D rotating sphere (tesseract-related geometry) to spark curiosity about non-Euclidean projections.

from manim import *
import numpy as np

class TeachingScene(Scene):
    def setup_layout(self, title_text, lecture_lines):
        # BASE
        self.camera.background_color = "#000000"
        self.title = Text(title_text, font_size=28, color=WHITE).to_edge(UP)
        self.add(self.title)

        # Left-side lecture content (bullets with "-")
        lecture_texts = [Text(line, font_size=22, color=WHITE) for line in lecture_lines]
        self.lecture = VGroup(*lecture_texts).arrange(DOWN, aligned_edge=LEFT).scale(0.8)
        self.lecture.to_edge(LEFT, buff=0.2)
        self.add(self.lecture)

        # Define fine-grained animation grid (4x4 grid on right side)
        self.grid = {}
        rows = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]  # Top to bottom
        cols = ["1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6"]  # Left to right

        for i, row in enumerate(rows):
            for j, col in enumerate(cols):
                x = 0.5 + j * 1
                y = 2.2 - i * 1
                self.grid[f"{row}{col}"] = np.array([x, y, 0])

    def place_at_grid(self, mobject, grid_pos, scale_factor=1.0):
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(self.grid[grid_pos])
        return mobject

    def place_in_area(self, mobject, top_left, bottom_right, scale_factor=1.0):
        tl_pos = self.grid[top_left]
        br_pos = self.grid[bottom_right]
        
        # Calculate center of the area
        center_x = (tl_pos[0] + br_pos[0]) / 2
        center_y = (tl_pos[1] + br_pos[1]) / 2
        center = np.array([center_x, center_y, 0])
        
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(center)
        return mobject
